title.text: Skids, braking technique and anti-lock brakes

why_how.text: Most skids come from a driver failing to adjust speed in time to road and traffic conditions such as snow, ice, rain, dirt, gravel and wet leaves, and cruise control must not be used in those conditions.

A rear wheel drive vehicle usually gives a feel of lost traction before a skid, but a front wheel drive may give no warning, and although front wheel drive handles better in snow its traction is not flawless, so its better feel must not tempt you to drive faster.

On a possibly slippery road drive slower, avoid sudden changes of speed or direction, slow by lifting off the gas, and if more slowing is needed squeeze the brakes with slow steady pressure, keep the wheels rolling, ease off if they begin to lock, and consider shifting to a lower gear.
With ordinary brakes on a slippery road you squeeze gently and ease off if the wheels lock, but with anti-lock brakes you hold steady pressure and never pump.
Skid prevention relies on gentle speed reduction, while skid recovery forbids braking altogether and depends on steering toward the intended path.
With anti-lock brakes use steady brake pressure and do not pump the brakes, following the owner's manual.

Skid recovery is the same for front and rear wheel drive: do not hit the brakes, which worsens the skid, steer in the direction you want the vehicle to go, and expect to steer left and right a few times before full control returns.

Stability control and similar improvements can help but never substitute for driver caution, four wheel and all wheel drive have better traction in snow but not on ice, and every driver should learn how the vehicle handles on ice or snow in an empty parking lot.
Anti-lock brakes let you brake and steer at the same time, and noise and vibration in the pedal are normal when they engage.

Pumping the brake or lifting your foot off the pedal disengages the anti-lock system, the owner's manual tells you whether the vehicle has it, and the anti-lock warning light shows briefly at start up.
A brief anti-lock light at start up is normal, while a light that stays lit while driving means the anti-lock function is lost even though normal braking remains.
If the anti-lock warning light stays on after you begin driving, the anti-lock system is not working, although the vehicle still has ordinary brakes.

why_how.text: In fog, heavy rain or heavy snow use low beam headlights, and the law requires headlights on whenever you cannot clearly see persons or vehicles five hundred feet ahead.

Studies show that driving with low beam headlights on in daytime reduces the risk of head on collisions by more than twenty percent, and daytime running lights that come on automatically must not be mistaken for headlights.
When snow, rain or fog limit visibility you must turn the headlights on, the best practice is to drive with at least low beams on even by day, and parking lights are only for a parked vehicle.

Night driving is more dangerous because you cannot see as far ahead, and the law requires headlights on from a half hour after sunset until a half hour before sunrise, so switch them on yourself because daytime running lights can make you think they already are.

The clock rule puts headlights on from a half hour after sunset to a half hour before sunrise, while the visibility rule requires them any time persons or vehicles cannot be seen five hundred feet ahead.
You always need to see four seconds ahead, and at night at forty miles per hour on low beams you are overdriving your headlights, unable to stop within the distance you can see.

Use high beams in open country with few other vehicles, keeping speed lower than by day even with them, and use low beams when approaching other vehicles or pedestrians, in areas with streetlights or fog, and when following another vehicle.
High beams belong on open country roads with few vehicles, while low beams are required when meeting, following, under streetlights or in fog, and daytime running lights are neither.

A courteous night driver promptly dims the headlights when meeting or following another vehicle, and to avoid being blinded by oncoming lights looks ahead toward the right edge of the road rather than directly at them.

title.text: Floods, barricades and water over the

why_how.text: Nationally, flash floods kill more people than any other weather event and nearly half of those deaths are vehicle related, so when hazardous driving conditions are forecast the best choice is to stay home and avoid unnecessary travel.

If a storm catches you on the road, slow down, switch cruise control off, stay alert, leave a gap of more than four seconds to the vehicle ahead, and take extra care at night or on roads you do not know.
Flood waters may wash away or undermine bridges, culverts and roadbeds, so never drive around traffic barricades or past road closed signs, and obey every detour sign.
Do not drive where water covers the road, because its depth is not obvious, it can hide washouts, and a vehicle's motor will stall in water, leaving you stranded or trapped.

Should your car stall in floodwater, leave it right away: rising water can sweep away a vehicle and its occupants, many fatalities happen while trying to move stalled cars, and even four inches of moving water impairs walking and conceals hazards.

Wind endangers all motorists but especially large vehicles and drivers towing trailers, so slower speeds are the best practice, and strong wind, heavy snow or ice can drop trees and wires into the road, which you must never approach or cross.
Check Weather Service flash flood and weather warnings and all hazardous driving notices before traveling.
